title: Wi-Fi Security: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Your Wi Fi has a password. But is it really safe? That depends entirely on which lock you're using.

lines.t: It depends which lock you use

scenes.heading: Hotel keys over the years
scenes.narration: Think of how hotel keys evolved. W E P was one metal key shared by every guest. Copy it once, and you can enter any room. W P A brought electronic locks with a new key per guest, but the cipher inside could still be picked. W P A two upgraded the lock to A E S, which is far tougher. But guests still shared one passphrase, so a weak one could be guessed offline. W P A three fixed that, and a stolen password no longer unlocks old traffic.

scenes.heading: WPA2 vs WPA3
scenes.narration: Here are the key differences. W P A two uses A E S with a hundred and twenty-eight bit key. W P A three moves to two fifty-six bit. W P A two Personal can be attacked offline if the passphrase is weak. W P A three uses S A E, which stops that.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. W P A three isn't backward compatible, though many access points offer a transition mode. Enterprise mode adds per user logins, but W P A three Personal can still be stronger in some ways. And W P A three still has a four way handshake, but it follows S A E.

items.right: Different strengths; WPA3 has forward secrecy

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva Wi-Fi security lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. W E P is broken. W P A uses T K I P. W P A two uses A E S. W P A three adds S A E and forward secrecy. Never use T K I P, and prefer W P A three. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva Wi-Fi security lab.

points.t: WEP broken, WPA TKIP, WPA2 AES
